title: Fenwick Tree (BIT)
why: Prefix sums that support point updates, in O(log n) each and about 10 lines. The go-to inversion counter and the cheapest way to get ordered-set rank queries.
checkpoint: You can count inversions in an array of 10^5 elements in O(n log n).

title: Segment Tree
why: Range query plus point update for any associative operation. More general than a Fenwick tree and the base for every advanced range structure above it.
checkpoint: You can build a segment tree for range-min and point-assign from memory.

title: Lazy Propagation
why: Range *update* plus range query, by deferring updates until a node is visited. The hard part is composing two pending updates correctly.
checkpoint: You can support range-add and range-sum on 10^5 elements with 10^5 queries.

title: Sqrt Decomposition
why: Split the array into sqrt(n) blocks for O(sqrt n) queries. Less powerful than a segment tree but far easier to adapt to strange operations.
checkpoint: You can answer range queries an operation that has no easy segment-tree merge.

title: Mo's Algorithm
why: Reorder offline queries so a moving window answers them all in O((n+q) sqrt n). The standard answer to 'count distinct in a range' with no updates.
checkpoint: You can answer 10^5 distinct-count range queries offline.

title: String Hashing
why: Compare any two substrings in O(1) with polynomial hashing. Use double hashing and a random base — single-mod hashes get hacked on Codeforces.
checkpoint: You can compare arbitrary substrings in O(1) and explain why you need two moduli.

title: KMP & Z-Function
why: Linear-time pattern matching, plus the prefix-function and Z-array as objects in their own right — they answer border, period, and occurrence-counting questions directly.
checkpoint: You can find all occurrences of a pattern in O(n+m) and compute all borders.

title: Trie
why: A prefix tree over strings — or over the bits of integers, which is how you solve maximum-XOR-pair problems.
checkpoint: You can find the maximum XOR pair in an array in O(n log C).

title: Strongly Connected Components
why: Condense a directed graph into a DAG of mutually reachable groups. Tarjan or Kosaraju; the condensation is what most problems actually want.
checkpoint: You can build the condensation DAG and run DP on it.

title: Bridges & Articulation Points
why: Edges and vertices whose removal disconnects the graph, via DFS entry times and low-links. Leads to bridge trees and biconnected components.
checkpoint: You can find all bridges in O(V+E) and build the bridge tree.

title: Small-to-Large & DSU on Tree
why: Answer subtree queries for every vertex in O(n log n) by always merging the smaller child's data into the larger. Deceptively simple, very powerful.
checkpoint: You can count distinct colours in every subtree in O(n log n).

title: Advanced Counting
why: Inclusion-exclusion, stars and bars, Catalan numbers, derangements, and the Burnside lemma — the vocabulary of harder counting problems.
checkpoint: You can apply inclusion-exclusion to a counting problem with 2^k terms.

title: Probability & Expected Value
why: Linearity of expectation is the key tool: sum per-element contributions instead of reasoning about whole outcomes. Expected values are usually output mod p as a fraction.
checkpoint: You can use linearity of expectation to avoid a state explosion.

title: Game Theory & Sprague-Grundy
why: Win/lose states, Nim, and the Grundy number that reduces any sum of independent games to a single XOR.
checkpoint: You can compute Grundy numbers for a game and solve its sum.

title: Divide & Conquer
why: Split, solve, and combine — merge-sort inversion counting, D&C over answer contributions, and the CDQ family.
checkpoint: You can count inversions with merge sort and explain the combine step.

title: Ternary Search
why: Find the extremum of a unimodal function. On integers, prefer binary search on the difference to avoid precision issues.
checkpoint: You can optimise a convex function and prove unimodality first.

title: Matrix Exponentiation
why: Any linear recurrence evaluated at index 10^18 in O(k^3 log n). Also computes path counts of fixed length in a graph.
checkpoint: You can compute the 10^18-th Fibonacci number mod p.

title: Interval DP
why: dp[l][r] over subintervals, combined at a split point — matrix chain multiplication, optimal BST, and the burst-balloons family. O(n^3) with an O(n^2) optimisation available via Knuth.
checkpoint: You can solve a matrix-chain-style problem in O(n^3).

title: Advanced Constructive
why: Harder invention problems: parity and invariant arguments, explicit constructions on graphs and grids, and proving impossibility.
checkpoint: You can identify an invariant that proves a case impossible.
